name: Square Suzanne-Buisson

beats.script_body: The most delightful approach to this corner of beauty on the hill of Montmartre is from the west: climb rue Caulaincourt from the Montmartre Cemetery, midway up take the stairs to the right onto avenue Junot, then a left into rue Simon Dereure, which ends in the charming Place-des-Quatre-Freres-Casadesus. The small steps to the right, through a rock garden, take you up to Square Suzanne-Buisson. You can sit and recover from the climb in the company of a few Parisians, pairs of friends or lovers, or grandparents keeping an eye on the children in the playground. Birds twitter and don't fly away, diving in and out of the trees, the wildflowers in the rock garden, circling the small greenhouse and the heights of the white mansions of Place Casadesus, home to generations of a family of great musicians.

beats.script_body: Near the front of the square a statue of Saint-Denis holds his severed head, overlooking the fountain and mall shaded by plane trees. According to legend, when Denis, the first bishop of Lutetia, was decapitated by the Romans, c. 258 AD — the site traditionally believed to be at the foot of the butte in rue Yvonne le Tac just east of Place des Abbesses — he carried his bloody head up to the spring that until the nineteenth century flowed here, washed it, and then continued north to the site of the Basilica of Saint-Denis, where he is buried. The origin of the name 'Montmartre' is commonly thought to be Mons Martyrum, after the story of the martyrdom of Denis and his two companions.

beats.script_body: The square is named for a victim of a modern totalitarian regime, Suzanne Levy Buisson, born in 1883. At the rue Girardin entrance, a 'Histoire de Paris' plaque identifies her as a martyr of the Resistance and secretary of the Women's Socialist Party. Arrested and tortured by the Nazis, she revealed nothing about the movement. Deported, she died in Germany, the date of her death not known. So little is known about Suzanne Buisson and the other Résistantes that her story and the near anonymity of the plaque's profile inject a dissonance into this hilltop place so filled with light.

beats.script_body: Standing at the entrance of the square, the author invokes Maurice Ravel, who knew Montmartre. In the face of a personal disaster, Ravel once said: 'I firmly believe that joy is far more fertile than pain.' In this Montmartre homage to the memory of Suzanne Buisson and Saint-Denis — in this pretty corner of Paris — there is in their courage a distinct vibration of joy.

name: Musée de Montmartre

beats.script_body: The approach to rue Cortot from the metro is an exhilarating and scenic climb up the Montmartre hill (butte): follow rue des Abbesses west, right to rue Tholoze, then right again into curvy rue Lepic — the old quarry road where Vincent Van Gogh lived with his brother Theo at number 54 in 1886–1888 and where the only windmills of Montmartre still stand — continue uphill along rue Norvins until the left downhill turn into rue des Saules of the willow trees, and, finally, right into the picturesque rue Cortot. The entrance to the garden is through the bookshop of the Musée de Montmartre.

beats.script_body: The loveliness of the garden's setting is matched by the museum itself — a seventeenth-century house first owned by an actor-colleague of Molière's. In spring its borders are thick with tulips, a softening grace under tall old trees. Beyond the lily pond and the rear garden are views of the small backyard gardens of rue Cortot and, below them, the Montmartre vineyards, parallel to rue des Saules — all of it feels like a generous reward for the rigors of the ascent, knowing you've escaped the crowds thronging Place du Tertre and the steps of Sacré-Coeur.

beats.script_body: In the Middle Ages, the abbesses of Montmartre owned huge estates up here. Henri IV occupied the original twelfth-century Benedictine Abbey — founded by Louis the Fat — during the Siege of Paris in 1589. His artillery dug in on the top of Montmartre as he bombarded the starving city below, which was defended from the Protestant Henri by armed monks and priests. 'My mistress — Paris — is very cruel to me,' he complained. Having neither wife nor mistress on hand, he seduced the Abbess Claude and another nun in his convent headquarters, rewarding them later with control of the abbeys of Vernon and Montmartre. Today the tiny restored church of Saint-Pierre de Montmartre, behind Sacré-Coeur, is the last surviving vestige of the great abbey where Henri IV flirted with the Catholic Church.

beats.source_passage: The museum offers sketchy details of the hill's history. In the Middle Ages, the abbesses of Montmartre owned huge estates up here. Henri IV occupied the original twelfth-century Benedictine Abbey (founded by Louis the Fat) during the Siege of Paris in 1589. His artillery dug in on the top of Montmartre as he bombarded the starving city below, which was defended from the Protestant Henri by armed monks and priests. 'My mistress'—Paris—'is very cruel to me,' he complained. Having neither wife nor mistress on hand, he seduced the Abbess Claude and another nun in his convent headquarters, rewarding them later with control of the abbeys of Vernon and Montmartre. Today the tiny (restored) church of Saint-Pierre de Montmartre, behind Sacre-Coeur, is the last surviving vestige of the great abbey where Henri IV flirted with the Catholic Church.

flagged_claims.note: The main Siege of Paris was 1590. Henri IV did conduct an initial assault in November 1589, but the prolonged siege was 1590. The book's '1589' refers to the start of Henri IV's campaign period. No auto-correction applied — this is a historian's distinction, not a clear error, and multiple sources support Henri IV using Montmartre as an artillery position.

fact_check.notes: Benedictine Abbey founded by Louis VI (Louis the Fat) confirmed. Henri IV's use of Montmartre for artillery confirmed. Abbess Claude de Beauvilliers confirmed.

beats.script_body: The museum also has a few remnants of 'Red Montmartre,' where the Paris Commune began in 1871. There's a bust of the Communards' emblematic heroine, Louise Michel (1830–1905), the schoolteacher who inspired the seventy-day resistance to the government's army and fought to claim the city for the people who had nothing. She read Baudelaire in the trenches, directed the construction and defense of the barricades, and led more than ten thousand women to fight with her during the bloody and brutal week — la semaine sanglante — of May 1871. Many artists and intellectuals supported the rebels or participated themselves in the civil war, including Courbet, Pissarro, Rimbaud, and Verlaine.

beats.script_body: Renoir lived in this house and knew the nearby moulins — used as dance halls by workers on weekends — painting the famous Bal du Moulin de la Galette in 1876 (now in the Musée d'Orsay). Raoul Dufy had his studio in the right wing in 1901. In Van Gogh's time, the hill was dotted with twenty-five windmills — moulins — which were being converted into dance halls and cabarets, a feature at the heart of Montmartre's reputation as a neighborhood of pleasure and adventure.

beats.script_body: Van Gogh saw desolation beneath the gaiety of Montmartre — a perception shared by his literary contemporaries, poets Paul Verlaine and Arthur Rimbaud and novelist Emile Zola. What did inspire Van Gogh was the panoramic prospect from the butte: the vast city below, often shrouded in fog and smoke, and the Seine running through it. The impressionists, in particular, were inspired by the rural atmosphere and the wide sky over the highest point in Paris.

name: Square Carpeaux

beats.script_body: Square Carpeaux — 'a people's park, the anti-Luxembourg,' according to one local — holds a statue of the sculptor Jean-Baptiste Carpeaux (1827–1875) surrounded by tall trees flush with singing birds, flower gardens, beds of shrubbery, a kiosk for local concerts, and a statue of a woman without an arm. A scene from Jean-Pierre Melville's Montmartre film Bob le flambeur takes place here, with the armless woman distinct in the background as Bob the compassionate crook talks business with a partner on a park bench.

beats.script_body: There is graffiti on a wall: 'Le peuple n'obtient que ce qu'il prend' — 'The people only get what they take.' Montmartre was from the first a neighborhood of workers, artisans, and the poor. It's mythologised now as a paradise of the well-heeled and successful artist — Picasso and company — but parts of it were always the territory of rebels, outsiders, and students who couldn't afford the rents in other parts of Paris.

beats.script_body: Square Léon-Serpollet is a people's garden built on terraces, on the former sites of artists' ateliers. It was built in memory of the children deported by the Vichy government under the German Occupation. The square opens onto the terraces through a pretty arbor and spreads out as you ascend, next to an elementary school. In nearby Place Pecqueur, a sculpted relief of an emigration scene by Steinlein stands watch.

name: Parc Turlure

beats.script_body: Parc Turlure sits north of Sacré-Coeur, where you hear nothing of the hordes and buses in front of it. The most scenic approach is along the village-like rue Saint-Vincent, past Au Lapin Agile — a cabaret-bar favored by Picasso, Modigliani, and Utrillo — uphill, past the beautiful intersection with rue Mont-Cenis framed by tall, elegant, ivy-covered mansions with a long view across northern canyons of steep steps, until you wind right into rue de la Bonne and the entrance to the park. With your back to the cascading artificial waterfall and Sacré-Coeur, you look out over the high brick mansions of Montmartre on the slopes below. Inside the shade of the arbor court, thick with greenery, there is silence and the fragrance of jasmine, which is everywhere.

beats.script_body: At the bottom of the steep, grassy hill beneath Sacré-Coeur, Square Louise-Michel is inscribed: 'Institutrice, Héroïne de la Commune de Paris.' Built into a circular staircase, a rich grove of trees — oranges des osages and chestnuts — surrounds the playground, a jubilant scene of music from the carousel and the camaraderie of children and parents from the surrounding multiethnic neighborhoods.

beats.source_passage: SQUARE LOUISE-MICHEL "Institutrice, Heroine de la Commune de Paris." At the bottom of the steep, grassy hill beneath Sacre-Coeur, usually a mob scene, the square is built into a circular staircase. A rich grove of trees—oranges des osages, chestnuts—surrounds the playground, a jubilant scene of music from the carousel and the camaraderie of children and parents from the surrounding multiethnic neighborhoods.

fact_check.notes: Louise Michel's schoolteacher identity and Commune role confirmed.

opening_hours_basis: Door; hours are the place's own OpenStreetMap tag: 08:00-17:45; PH,Sa,Su 08:00-09:00 off, Mar 01-Mar Su[-1] 17:45-19:00, Oct 01-Oct Su[-1] 17:45-19:30, Mar Su[-1]-Apr 30,Sep 17:45-20:30, May 01-Aug 31 17:45-21:30.
visit_basis: The formal stepped garden below Sacré-Cœur, tiered lawns, a fountain and the panoramic view of Paris; you climb the terraces and stand at the belvedere, an open landscaped slope with nothing to enter.
judgement_basis: The stepped terraced lawns below Sacré-Coeur are steep and busy with dense tourist crowds rather than free running ground, but there are wide steps and grass to sit on and it is a large open unfenced space, lit and thronged with people late into the evening.
queue_basis: The open terraced garden below Sacré-Cœur is entered freely from the street with no gate or check, so no line exists.

name: Square des Abbesses

beats.script_body: A few steps north of metro Abbesses is the little square with the charming Je t'aime Wall — written 311 times in 250 languages on an enameled fresco made of 612 tiles. The fragments of color represent the pieces of a broken heart.

opening_hours_basis: A fenced Paris municipal square with closing gates, but its specific hours are not confidently known; gated, hours not confidently known; left unfiltered.
visit_basis: Small Montmartre square by the Art Nouveau metro entrance and the church, with the wall of love nearby; you circle the space taking in the metro canopy and facades, nothing entered here.
judgement_basis: A small fenced garden beside the Abbesses metro with traffic-free paths and lawn where children can run and benches quiet enough to talk, but a gated square locked after dark.
queue_basis: A small public square-garden entered through an open gate with no ticket, so there is no queue to price.

name: Montmartre Cemetery
short_description: Atmospheric cemetery in the 18th arrondissement with graves of Alexandre Dumas, Degas, Dalida, Berlioz, and Francois Truffaut

beats.script_body: Here lie Stendhal, Berlioz, Julie Récamier, Heinrich Heine, and Fragonard, under the linden trees, where Colette used to roam and gather flowers. German students come looking for the grave of Heine. Truffaut (1932–1984), who grew up in Montmartre, is buried here. A scene in The 400 Blows takes place on the bridge over the cemetery that leads up rue Caulaincourt to Square Suzanne-Buisson.

opening_hours_basis: A gated walled cemetery with closing gates; hours follow the City of Paris's published summer pattern shared across municipal cemeteries.
visit_basis: Mid-size terraced cemetery with several notable graves along tree-lined paths; explored on foot outdoors with no interior.
judgement_basis: A solemn walled cemetery where running and noise are out of place, with quiet benches where two can talk, but its gates are locked at night leaving no one able to stand inside.
queue_basis: A free public cemetery entered through open gates with no ticketing or bag check, so there is no line to join.

name: Lapin Agile
short_description: Surviving Montmartre cabaret on the slope behind Sacré-Cœur, taking its name from André Gill's 1875 painted sign of a rabbit leaping from a saucepan and immortalized by Picasso's 1905 painting.
opening_hours_basis: Door; hours are the place's own OpenStreetMap tag: Tu,Th-Sa 21:00-01:00.
visit_basis: Historic Montmartre cabaret; the painted rabbit sign and ivy-clad exterior take a few minutes, while an actual evening show inside runs well past two hours and is capped at the 90-minute tour maximum.
judgement_basis: A cabaret on a steep Montmartre lane with no enclosed traffic-free ground, no free public seating (only ticketed indoor seats), and its sloping side street is dim and largely deserted at night, so someone left standing there is not fine.
queue_basis: A small cabaret admitted by a single door at the start of an evening show, so a brief cluster forms at doors-open time but there is no security screening or all-day line.
